options.why: The gateway gives the multifactor protection the application itself cannot provide, which is compensating.

options.t: It records each sign-in for later review
options.why: The gateway enforces a second factor; it does not only record sign-ins.

options.t: It tells staff how to sign in safely
options.why: Users are not just told what to do; the gateway enforces the second factor.

detail: its old billing application cannot support it
explain: A gateway that enforces multifactor sign-in for a system that cannot support it addresses the same risk by other means, which is compensating.

stem: A facilities manager at a translation agency must add badge readers to every server room door under the company's security standard. The lease of the office building forbids any wiring through the doors, so under an approved exception the manager instead keeps the servers in locked cabinets whose keys sit in a logged key safe.
ask: Which of the following control types do the locked cabinets provide in this case?

options.why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The cabinets stand in for the badge readers the lease does not allow, guarding the same servers.
The cabinets physically keep people out; they are not instructions to staff.
The cabinets are not there to discourage anyone; they replace the required readers.

detail: The lease of the office building forbids any wiring through the doors
explain: When the control a standard requires cannot be installed for a business reason, an approved substitute that reduces the same risk is a compensating control.

stem: A small clinic's insurer requires that any after-hours entry to the records room be detected and answered within minutes, and suggests a night guard, which the clinic cannot afford. With the insurer's written approval, the office manager instead installs a door alarm monitored by a firm that sends a responder within minutes.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the alarm in this case?

options.why: The alarm meets the same requirement the guard would have met, in place of a guard the clinic cannot afford.
The alarm detects entry, but it was put in place instead of the required guard and meets that guard's requirement.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The alarm does not tell anyone what to do.

detail: which the clinic cannot afford
edge: An alarm detects entry, but this one was installed in place of the guard the clinic cannot afford and meets the same stated requirement, which makes it compensating.
explain: A control used instead of one that cannot be put in place, meeting the same requirement to a comparable degree, is compensating. The alarm also detects, but its role here is the approved substitute.

stem: An auditor at a museum reads the exception record below.
ask: Which of the following describes the in_place_instead line?

lines: required: full-disk encryption on all devices
asset: GALLERY-KIOSK-2 (hardware cannot support encryption)
in_place_instead: no visitor data stored locally, kiosk bolted to the wall
review: quarterly

options.t: A repair made after an earlier incident
options.why: No incident is recorded; nothing is being repaired.
The line lists measures in place, not instructions to staff.

options.t: A substitute for a missing safeguard
options.why: The line lists what stands in for the encryption the kiosk cannot support, which is compensating.
Nothing in the line identifies or records events.

detail: hardware cannot support encryption
explain: An exception record names the required control, why it cannot be used and what stands in for it. The stand-in is the compensating control.

stem: A risk analyst at a logistics firm reviews a colleague's summary of compensating controls.
ask: Which of the following statements in the summary are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: It is applied after an incident to restore systems
options.why: Restoring after an incident is corrective.

options.t: It addresses the same risk as the missing control
options.why: A compensating control must give similar protection against the same risk.

options.t: It is any cheaper control chosen to save money
options.why: It must address the same risk to a comparable degree; cost alone does not make one.

options.t: It is often temporary until the ideal control is possible
options.why: It is often a stand-in until the system can take the ideal control.

options.t: It only tells staff what they should do
options.why: Telling staff what to do is directive.

detail: reviews a colleague's summary of compensating controls
explain: A compensating control substitutes for one that cannot be used, gives similar protection, and is often temporary. It is not the same as corrective.

ask: Which of the following explains how a directive control works?

options.t: It enforces a rule so no one can break it
options.why: Enforcing so the act cannot happen is preventive.

options.t: It instructs people and relies on compliance
options.why: Directive controls tell people what to do and rely on them to comply.

options.t: It warns of consequences to discourage misuse
options.why: Warning of consequences to discourage misuse describes a deterrent control.

options.t: It restores systems after an incident has happened
options.why: Restoring after an incident is corrective.

explain: A directive control tells people what they should or should not do. It does not enforce the rule, so it works only as far as people comply.

ask: Which of the following controls is directive?

options.t: A door that locks itself whenever it closes
options.why: A self-locking door blocks entry, which is preventive.

options.t: A sign warning that trespassers will be prosecuted
options.why: Warning of consequences is deterrent.

options.t: An alarm that sounds when a door opens
options.why: An alarm identifies an event, which is detective.

options.t: A policy telling staff where to store files
options.why: A policy that states required behavior is directive.

explain: Policies and instructional signs are directive controls. They tell people what to do but enforce nothing.

stem: A contractor visiting a pharmaceutical plant sees a sign at a lab door reading 'Lab staff only beyond this point.' The door itself is not locked.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sign provide?

options.why: The door is not locked, so nothing stops anyone entering.
The sign names no consequence; it only says who may enter.
The sign records nothing and raises no alert.
The sign tells people who may enter and relies on them to comply.

detail: Lab staff only beyond this point
explain: An instructional sign is directive: it says what people should do. A sign warning of consequences would lean deterrent instead.

stem: A newspaper's handbook says reporters must lock their screens whenever they step away from their desks. The computers do not lock by themselves.
ask: Which of the following control types does the handbook rule provide?

options.why: Nothing locks the screens automatically, so nothing is blocked.
The rule tells reporters what to do and relies on them to do it.
No consequence is stated; the handbook only says what to do.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

detail: The computers do not lock by themselves
explain: A rule that instructs but does not enforce is directive. A screen that locked itself would be the preventive version.

stem: A forklift trainer at a warehouse points out two signs near the racking. One reads 'Forklift drivers only beyond the yellow line.' The other reads 'Violators will be fined.'
ask: Which of the following control types does the first sign provide?

options.why: The first sign says who may go where and relies on compliance.
That fits the second sign, which warns of a fine.
A sign stops no one crossing the line.
Neither sign records anything.

detail: Forklift drivers only beyond the yellow line
explain: Directive instructs; deterrent warns of consequences. The first sign instructs, and the second warns of a fine.

stem: The office manager at a design studio notes that the studio's acceptable use policy forbids installing unapproved apps. Later, the studio adds a tool that refuses to run any app not on an approved list.
ask: Which of the following control types does the acceptable use policy provide?

options.why: That fits the tool that refuses unapproved apps, not the policy.
The policy records nothing and raises no alert.
The policy states required behavior and relies on staff to comply.
The policy repairs nothing after an event.

detail: acceptable use policy forbids installing unapproved apps
explain: A policy that forbids something is directive; a tool that actually blocks it is preventive. The stem describes both, and asks about the policy.

stem: The vendor manager at a bank adds a clause to the contract with its cloud provider requiring the provider to keep the bank's data only in data centers inside the country.
ask: Which of the following control types does the contract clause provide?

options.why: The clause discovers nothing; it states a duty.
The clause states what the provider must do and relies on it to comply.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.
Nothing in the clause technically stops the data from being moved; it relies on the provider to comply.

detail: requiring the provider to keep the bank's data only in data centers inside the country
explain: A contract clause that requires behavior from a vendor is directive: it states the rule and relies on compliance.

stem: An airline's policy says staff must not share their accounts. Nothing in its systems blocks sharing, and auditors later find shared accounts in several teams.
ask: Which of the following explains why the policy did not stop the sharing?

options.t: It relies on people choosing to comply
options.why: A directive control instructs but does not enforce, so people can ignore it.

options.t: It acts only after the sharing happens
options.why: Acting after an event describes a corrective control, not a policy.

options.t: It records sharing but raises no alert
options.why: A policy records nothing; recording an event would be detective.

options.t: It stands in for a missing control
options.why: Standing in for a missing control describes compensating, not this policy.

detail: Nothing in its systems blocks sharing
explain: Directive controls instruct but do not enforce, so they work only as far as people comply. With nothing blocking it, the sharing went on.

stem: The receptionist at a marine supply company receives the notice below.
ask: Which of the following control types does the notice provide?

lines: From: security@harbor.example
To: all staff
From Monday, every visitor must be signed in at the front desk and escorted at all times.

options.why: The notice states no consequence for ignoring it.
Nothing in the notice physically stops an unescorted visitor.
The notice records nothing.
The notice tells staff what must happen and relies on them to comply.

detail: every visitor must be signed in at the front desk and escorted
explain: A notice stating required behavior is directive. Other controls, such as a front desk check, would be needed to enforce it.

stem: The compliance lead at a tax advisory firm wants to add two directive controls for how staff handle client tax returns.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.t: A lock on the cabinet holding paper returns
options.why: A lock stops anyone without a key from opening the cabinet, which is preventive.

options.t: A log that records each return a user opens
options.why: A log records what happened, which is detective.

options.t: A policy to save returns only in the protected folder
options.why: A policy tells staff where to save returns and relies on them to comply, which is directive.

options.t: A notice warning that leaks will be prosecuted
options.why: A warning of consequences is deterrent.

options.t: A guide listing the steps for emailing returns securely
options.why: A guide tells staff what to do and relies on them to follow it, which is directive.

detail: two directive controls
explain: Directive controls instruct: a policy on where returns are saved and a guide to sending them. The lock prevents, the log detects and the notice deters.
